1. . Agreement on basic terminology of:

  - **Current Data** means that data is equivalent to the results of logical view execution as of now.
  - **Fresh Data** means that max_staleness policy is satisfied (data may not need to be current)

2. There is general agreement not to differentiate Schema staleness vs data staleness. If nested views changed schema on nested tables have data, we consider them as changes and do not differentiate between them from the max_Staleness calculation perspective (obvious exception to the top level materialized view itself, it’s metadata, and definition needs to be older then the last refresh) .. .

3. Long discussion on Document above.

There is general agreement on the Time-Based Check section.

General general agreement  on  Scenarios for different Refresh Behavior sectionthe

There is disagreement on the  Staleness definition,

 Two competing definitions:

  - Max staleness window starts at a point of refresh and goes forward. Results are considered Fresh if they either pass Time-Based Check or data is Current.
  - Max Staleness window: results considered fresh if it represents a view of the source data from a specific point in time within the allowed max_staleness window: [now-max_staleness, now].

AI :

Daniel and Igor will work out crisp definitions for both options with examples.

body:
([recording](https://youtu.be/LAagm_DTGgI))

Agenda

  - Max staleness window for logic check

      - Look ahead from the start of the last refresh
      - Look back from now
  - PoC/implementations

Notes:

  - Reviewed current engine behaviors for staleness config

      - BigQuery has the max_staleness config with the lookback behavior
      - Trino has staleness/grace period config wi the look-ahead behavior
      - Dremio has the staleness config with only time-based check
      - StarRocks has a mv_rewrite_staleness_second config with look ahead behavior
      - Snowflake dynamic table doesn’t have the staleness config. It has a target lag as a hint to refresh intervals. There is no guarantee on the refresh completion. Materializations are always good to be consumed.
      - Postgres doesn’t have the staleness config. Materialized views are always good to be consumed.
      - Redshift doesn’t have the staleness config. Direct query of MVs are always good to consume the materializations. Automatic query rewrite would ensure the materializations are the same as executing the view SQL directly.
  - Considering the diverse engine behavior, max staleness config would add non-trivial complexity to the MV spec. There are supports on dropping the max staleness config in MV spec and just follow the Postgres behavior.
  - Arguments to support having the max staleness config is that some engines have this concept. Freshness evaluation is a key component of MV. It will be good to have some boundary and defined behavior in the MV spec. To support the diverse behavior, maybe the spec can allow client flexibility for the freshness evaluation

      - Every client is required to implement the time based check. This is the simplest and most strict form of interpretation. Additionally, clients may perform one of the next two logic checks.
      - Look ahead window
      - Look back window (delayed view semantics)
  - Igor will try to write down some description and see if the writing can capture the flexibility without confusions. We will review it in the next meeting.

—-----------------

[BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/materialized-views-create#max_staleness)

  - If the last refresh occurred within the max_staleness interval, then BigQuery returns data directly from the materialized view without reading the base tables. For example, this applies if your max_staleness interval is 4 hours, and the last refresh occurred 2 hours ago.
  - If the last refresh occurred outside the max_staleness interval, then BigQuery reads the data from the materialized view, combines it with changes to the base table since the last refresh, and returns the combined result. This combined result might still be stale, up to your max_staleness interval. For example, this applies if your max_staleness interval is 4 hours, and the last refresh occurred 7 hours ago.

Redshift has no max staleness config (AI summary)

  - Strict fresh requirement for automatic query rewrite
  - Permissive for direct MV query

[StarRocks](https://docs.starrocks.io/docs/sql-reference/sql-statements/materialized_view/CREATE_MATERIALIZED_VIEW/)

  - Mv_rewrite_staleness_second If the materialized view's last refresh is within the time interval specified in this property, this materialized view can be used directly for query rewrite, regardless of whether the data in the base tables changes. If the last refresh is before this time interval, StarRocks checks whether the base tables have been updated to determine whether the materialized view can be used for query rewrite.

body:
([recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcauEm30nX8))

Agenda

  - Max staleness config needed or not? if yes, what are the allowed semantics?
  - PoC/implementations

Notes

  - Agreed to drop the max stateless config and the definition of staleness evaluation because reconciling the different semantics from various database/engine behaviors is difficult.
  - Keep the “refresh-state” list that the producer populates.

      - It is up to the producer to determine what to populate in the list. E.g. The producer can decide whether to include nested tables.
      - A producer can leverage the refresh state to implement incremental refresh
      - The refresh state can also allow the consumer to perform a staleness check (using whatever semantics the consumer chooses). E.g., a consumer can strictly check if the source tables have any data changes compared to the refresh state. A consumer can just always read the storage table and implicitly trust the producer for the storage table refresh.
  - It is up to the engine to express storage table layout configs (like partitioning, sort order) in the “CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW” DDL and carry it over to the storage table creation.
  - Materialized view loading would need 3 round trips: load table (failed), load view, load storage table. This will be the starting point.

      - We can have a separate discussion on how to improve this in the future. E.g., REST catalog can have a universal load endpoint for (table, view, MV) for a single resource or a batch of resources.
      - When loading a MV, REST catalog may even piggyback the source tables/views in the same response to save the client a 2nd round trip to fetch source table states. This assumes the catalog can understand the view SQL.
      - A universal load endpoint may be natural for the REST catalog. We should also look into engine integration. E.g., engines may have separate table and view catalogs and thus can’t leverage the universal load endpoint. What complexity is required for engines to evolve to take advantage of the universal load endpoint (if available)?

The storage table refewrence field in the view definition can be relied on to distinguish whether the view is a logical or materialized view. There is no need for a separate \`isMaterialized\` boolean flag. With that, engines don't need to persist storage table configs (like partitioning, sort order) in the view properties.
  - We are not aware of any engine that supports DDL that converts a logical view to a materialized view. Clients can still call the SDK (like Java) to convert a logical view to a materialized view by (1) create a storage table (2) update the view definition with the storage table reference.
